newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE-China's Xichang hopes for more satellite launches.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-China's Xichang hopes for more satellite launches.

text.p: Water buffalo still stroll outside the remote Xichang Satellite Launching Centre and poor peasant farmers eke an existence from small fields scattered around its perimeter fence.
But China hopes the technology inside its space city will propel it to the forefront of the world's lucrative commercial satellite launch business.
The launch centre, nestled in a green, tree-lined valley in southwestern Sichuan province, has launched more than 20 satellites since the mid-1980s.
However, two spectacular and deadly launch explosions in 1995 and 1996 tarnished China's reputation as a cheap but reliable alternative to France, Russia and other international competitors.
CHINA SAYS THERE ARE NO PROBLEMS

Those setbacks have left officials reluctant to give details of their ambitious space programme, although they stood firmly behind the technology of the new generation Long March 3B rocket -- the future hope of China's satellite launching programme.
"I think the problems have been solved," said Mao Di, chief engineer for the Xichang Satellite Launching Centre. "The Long March 3B is reliable."

The eyes of the world will be on Xichang this month when it launches a satellite for the Philippines in the first known use of the Long March 3B rocket since it exploded on its maiden flight in February 1996.
Officials insisted a flurry of activity had already begun in preparation for the launch.

But outside the building at the heart of the military base that houses part of mission control it was business as usual as a souvenir stand sold plastic model rockets to tourists for eight yuan ($1) apiece.
Xichang stands to lose a lot more than tourist revenue if the coming launch fails, since launch fees typically run into millions of dollars, industry sources said.
The heart of China's satellite launching programme is hidden in an unprepossessing, three-storey building that could be mistaken for a school were it not for the soldiers standing guard.
Inside, chief engineer Mao showed off the banks of screens and other instruments that allow ground control to monitor launches, and to gather and analyse data.

At one of the site's launching pads, another official voiced confidence in the Long March 3B, a three-stage, liquid-fuelled rocket that hurls satellites into space with the help of four strap-on boosters.
"I think it's okay," said the official. "The structure (of the Long March 3B) is pretty good."
Insurance companies are not so sure, and premiums to insure satellites that use Chinese carriers have soared since the recent setbacks.

All launch sites carry their own particular set of problems and Xichang's location in the rugged mountains of Sichuan has meant that weather and satellite positioning are concerns, said one industry source.
"It doesn't take a lot of rain or wind to call a launch off," he said. "And the further a site is from the equator, the harder and more expensive it is to put a satellite into the correct orbit."
TWO COMPANIES CONFIDENT

Filipino satellite company Mabuhay and Beijing-controlled Hong Kong firm APT Satellite Holdings Ltd have demonstrated their confidence in China by scheduling launches for August and September, two of Xichang's six commercial launches scheduled for this year.
"After looking at everything, finally we decided to go with the Chinese launcher," said one official from Mabuhay, who added that cost had not been the major consideration.

At the launch site, visitors gawked at a 76-metre (249-ft) structure built in the early 1980s for launching rockets with lighter payloads, as well as a 97-metre (318-ft) tower dating from the late 1980s and used for bigger rockets.
Although the authorities block access to the site during launches, houses of local residents stand close to the entrance of the launching pad -- sometimes with fatal consequences.
In January 1995, a Long March 2E rocket carrying the original Apstar 2 satellite blew up, killing a family of six in a rain of fiery debris.
In February of the following year, the first Long March 3B rocket exploded, killing at least six people and destroying the U.S.-built Intelsat 708 satellite.
That was followed last August by the failure of a Long March 3 rocket to put its Chinasat-7 orbiter into the proper orbit.
Beijing's two domestic comeback launches this year, a weather satellite aboard a Long March 3 and a communications orbiter on a 3A, have boosted international confidence, industry sources say.
But whether China will succeed in reaching for the stars -- and winning foreign orders -- will depend on this month's launch.
